justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term outlook with gradual drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and typical overnight drift would keep the asset near its recent trading range, with only a slight upward nudge reflecting mild positive momentum. For the one-week estimate, I extended that modest drift slightly further, acknowledging that short-term trends tend to persist weakly but that reversion forces also build. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate moves only marginally higher, reflecting the general long-run upward bias embedded in equity-like assets balanced against the realistic possibility of consolidation or modest pullback after any recent run-up.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects fundamental uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because intraday and overnight price movements in a liquid asset tend to be bounded absent a major catalyst. By one week, macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and sector-specific news can meaningfully shift prices, so I widened the band accordingly. At one month, the interval nearly doubles in width, capturing the full range of plausible macro regimes, earnings surprises, geopolitical developments, and shifting market sentiment that could materialize over a four-week window.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected hawkish policy surprise from a major central bank, a sudden deterioration in credit conditions, or a geopolitical shock could drive prices well below the lower bound of the monthly interval. Liquidity events or a broader risk-off episode driven by systemic concerns — such as a banking stress resurgence or sovereign credit fears — represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data print, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices meaningfully above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where momentum can amplify initial moves.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals are calibrated under relatively normal market conditions and assume no structural break in the underlying dynamics. If regime-changing information emerges — a major merger, regulatory action, or an unprecedented macro event — all three horizons could be invalidated simultaneously. The stated 90% confidence intervals are honest attempts at calibration, but they implicitly assume the distribution of outcomes resembles the recent historical distribution, which is itself a fragile assumption when conditions are shifting.
